title: Anthropic replaces Git with in-house Scion as agent-written code pushes merges to 30,000 a day
subtitle: The company's engineering team describes a changeset-based, server-side version control system built in five months after monthly merge volume rose roughly 12x — a concrete look at what AI-scale developer infrastructure actually looks like.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic published an engineering post on October 13 titled 'Redesigning Source Control,' describing Scion, an in-house version control system that replaced Git for the company's monorepo. The team cites a specific trigger: daily merge volume rose from roughly 2,500 in May 2026 to more than 30,000 in September, the bulk of which was Claude-written code committed through agent workflows. Git's assumptions — local-first, commit-granularity history, filesystem-shaped checkouts — stopped scaling to that cadence, and a seven-person team migrated the monorepo in five months.

Scion uses changesets rather than Git commits, and moves the heavy work — commit construction and merging — to the server rather than the client. According to the engineering post, that single architectural choice shrinks the local footprint by roughly 200x compared to the previous Git mirroring setup, drops checkout times from minutes to seconds, and raises CI capacity by about 25%. Each cache tier reportedly maintains more than 99% hit rates. Anthropic also built a companion code review tool called Antique, plus internal code search and access controls, as part of the same redesign.

The company is explicit that Scion is not a general-purpose Git replacement, and will not be open-sourced in its current form. The post frames it as a set of design ideas others could apply inside their own Git setups, not a product. The honest subtext is that most organizations do not have a merge-volume problem that justifies this; the ones that will — commercial labs, large-scale agent fleets, enterprises letting Claude or Codex commit directly — need to see where the bottleneck actually lives, which is build systems, CI, and merge resolution, not editors or inference.

For learners: the practical lesson is that agentic coding breaks tooling long before it breaks the model. If you are evaluating where to invest effort as an early-career engineer, the gap between 'LLMs can write code' and 'organizations can safely absorb LLM-written code at volume' is where almost all the real engineering is happening right now. Read the Anthropic post itself, not the summaries — the specific numbers (12x in four months, 200x footprint, 99%+ cache hit rate) are more informative than the headline.
